line_or_sentence: l.56 (''Type III'' paragraph), repeated at l.107; also sections/s03d_admiss.tex l.34 and sections/s17_open.tex l.95
manuscript_claim: ''its thermal signals have no finite propagation speed in the strict sense, since the strongly damped wave equation has a parabolic smoothing effect''
what_source_says: Green & Naghdi themselves state the opposite in footnote 2, p.190: ''both types II and III theories for heat flow in a stationary rigid solid accommodate finite wave speed, only type II involves no energy dissipation''. The type III equation is a damped wave equation whose principal part is hyperbolic, so the signal speed is c_* = sqrt(k*/rho c); what is lost is a sharp front, not finite speed. Parabolic smoothing of the amplitude is not the same as infinite propagation speed. The same paragraph concedes that ''statements in the literature that type III has a finite thermal wave speed should be read as referring to the undamped limit'' without citing who says it
source_ref: Green & Naghdi 1993, J. Elasticity 31:189-208, footnote 2, p.190 (read in the PDF)

manuscript_claim: ''their restrictions d alpha - h >= 0, h > 0 (Eqs. (4.14) and (4.16) of that paper) give the ordering stated''
what_source_says: The copy read (J. Elasticity 2(1):1-7, 1972) yielded text only up to §2; the abstract states the symmetric heat-conduction tensor and second-sound effects but not these inequalities. The equation numbers and the identifications tau_1 = alpha (coefficient of theta-dot in the stress) and tau_0 = h/d could not therefore be checked against the source

line_or_sentence: l.30 (Table: heat-law properties, GL row); same wording in sections/s03_foundations.tex l.73
what_source_says: The abstract does attribute the restrictions to an entropy-production inequality, which supports the provenance. But the ordering tau_1 >= tau_0 is not in the part of the paper that was read, and sections/s03_foundations.tex l.73 correctly notes that ''the original paper expresses this through constitutive coefficients and does not name a relaxation time''; the tau_0, tau_1 names are the manuscript's relabelling, which the sentence understates

manuscript_claim: ''the fitted second-sound speed at 85 K is about 3200 m/s against 3650 m/s from ab initio calculations, with oscillations at 104 and 125 K and none at 50 and 150 K''
what_source_says: The abstract of the first-release version (14 March 2019) reports only that second sound was observed above 100 K in qualitative agreement with ab initio calculations; none of the four numbers appears in it. The manuscript does flag them as ''values from the first-release version ... with no error bar quoted for the fit'', which is consistent with what the PDF is, but the values themselves were not verified because the results section was not read
source_ref: Science, DOI 10.1126/science.aav3548; abstract, p.1 of first release

line_or_sentence: l.15 (''Why the truncation order matters for stability'')
manuscript_claim: ''Quintanilla derived the condition tau_T > tau_q/2 (exponential stability, with instability for tau_T < tau_q/2) by a spectral argument, for the version in which the flux is expanded to second order in tau_q and the gradient to first order in tau_T, that is, variant (ii)''
what_source_says: Accurate and correctly scoped: the paper states ''when t_gamma > t_q/2 the solutions decay exponentially and when t_gamma < t_q/2 there exist unstable solutions'', and it works with the flux expanded to second order in the heat-flux lag. Recorded here because the manuscript's restriction to one truncation is exactly the source's own limitation, so the sentence should not later be widened to the whole DPL template
source_ref: Quintanilla 2003, J. Thermal Stresses 26(7):713-721, abstract and Eq. (1), p.713

manuscript_claim: ''Chen derives ballistic-diffusive equations from the Boltzmann equation in the relaxation-time approximation''
what_source_says: Accurate: the paper introduces ''new heat-conduction equations, named ballistic-diffusive equations, which are derived from the Boltzmann equation'' under the relaxation-time approximation, Eq. (1). No correction needed; recorded as a checked row
source_ref: Phys. Rev. Lett. 86(11):2297 (2001); abstract and Eq. (1), p.2297

manuscript_claim: cited as the review of the heat-pulse experiments
what_source_says: Accurate: the paper presents the phonon extended thermodynamics as a unified theory and claims ''a full explanation of the observations of the heat-pulse experiments in which ballistic phonons, second sound and ordinary heat conduction compete''. No correction needed
